tldr: By training on three simple simulated interaction models—a virtual spring, plane, and rail—the authors created a "reflex policy" that complies with the environment and caps contact forces without any force sensors.
hero_caption: An overview of the proposed approach. A reflex policy is pre-trained in simulation using three interaction primitives: a spring, a plane, and a rail (bottom). It is inserted as a frozen intermediate layer between the high-level controller and the joint control layer (C). In dual-arm box lifting (A) and tight-clearance peg insertion (B), it absorbs command errors and safely caps contact forces.
overview:
In contact-rich manipulation where robots touch and interact with objects, contact itself provides valuable cues about local geometry. However, end-effector trajectories commanded by high-level motion planners or RL policies inevitably suffer from object misalignments or perception errors. Trying to track these directly with standard position control or stiff impedance control leads to excessive contact forces. This can damage the robot or workpiece, or cause the arm to jam and stop.

To address this, the authors designed a framework to learn a "reflex policy." Without relying on force sensors or prior 3D meshes of the environment, it relieves local contact forces using only proprioception (the history of joint angles and tracking errors). Crucially, the policy is not trained on full, task-specific environments. Instead, it experiences only three simple virtual constraints in simulation: a spring, a plane, and a rail. By penalizing excessive contact forces, it learns ahead of time to offset joint targets in directions that yield to contact.

The trained reflex policy was deployed as a frozen execution layer and tested on humanoid dual-arm box lifting, high-precision peg insertion with a tight 0.02 mm clearance, and rough-surface following over unknown terrain. Even when commands penetrated deeply into objects, it consistently kept contact forces below preset thresholds. In peg insertion, it substantially improved real-world success rates compared to conventional controllers. This demonstrates the practical value of a new robot control architecture that, once trained, can be reused across diverse tasks and high-level planners.
contributions: Proposing a simulation-training framework that learns a general-purpose, contact-relieving reflex policy using only three simple geometric interaction primitives: a spring, a plane, and a rail.

Correcting target joint commands to respect contact force thresholds using only a 0.5-second proprioceptive history (joint positions and command tracking errors), without explicit force sensors such as 6-axis F/T sensors.

Demonstrating both compliant behavior and low contact forces across diverse real-world and simulated tasks—dual-arm lifting, 0.02 mm clearance peg insertion, and unknown rough-surface following—by embedding the trained reflex policy as a frozen execution layer.

sections.heading: Turning contact into an ally: Why do we need a reflexive intermediate layer?
sections.summary: Contact-rich tasks require moving along environmental geometric constraints, but commands from high-level planners inherently carry errors. This paper inserts a proprioceptive reflex policy, trained on simple interaction primitives, between high-level commands and joint control to prevent excessive contact forces while preserving task intent.
sections.details:
When a robot assembles parts or traces a surface, environmental features like walls or grooves serve as guides. Sliding along a plane or funneling a peg into a hole can compensate for minor perception errors.

However, commands generated by high-level motion planners, learned policies, or teleoperation rarely match exact real-world geometry. For example, commanding an end-effector deep inside an object during surface exploration causes severe reaction forces under standard position control or stiff impedance control (a classic control method assigning stiffness to yield under force). This can trigger oscillations, instability, or hardware damage.

To address this, this research trains an intermediate execution layer (a reflex policy) via reinforcement learning—resembling a human tendon reflex—that respects high-level intent while yielding locally to prevent excessive force. As shown in Fig. 1(A), even when high-level commands penetrate deeply into a box, the reflex layer pulls joint targets back toward the surface to prevent over-squeezing. Training uses no complex task environments, relying exclusively on minimal primitives: a virtual spring, plane, and rail.

captions.F1: System overview. (A) Dual-arm humanoid box lifting: standard inverse kinematics (IK) places targets deep inside the box, but the reflex policy pulls targets back near the surface. (B) High-precision peg insertion setup. (C) Hierarchical control architecture placing the reflex layer between high-level commands and the joint controller, alongside the three virtual interaction primitives (spring, plane, rail) used for training (bottom).

sections.heading: Exploiting environmental constraints and the lineage of learned interaction control
sections.summary: A review of classic impedance control, environmental constraint primitives, and reinforcement learning with force thresholds. The proposed method unifies these concepts as a general-purpose execution layer that corrects joint targets directly from proprioceptive history without force sensors.
sections.details:
### Environmental Constraints and Compliant Control
Leveraging Environmental Constraints (EC) to achieve manipulation tasks has a long history. Classical impedance and admittance control (methods that adapt target trajectories based on external forces) define relationships between tracking error and contact force. However, dynamically tuning stiffness or force-control axes for unknown geometry is notoriously difficult.

### Learning-Based Interaction Control
Recently, reinforcement learning has been applied to regulate contact forces. For instance, FORGE trains assembly policies that penalize contact forces exceeding maximum allowable limits. Other methods generate target positions satisfying static impedance relationships using joint tracking delay history without force sensors. Building on these insights, this work differs by learning a reflex layer that acts as a generic substrate beneath any task, rather than solving a single assembly task.

### Proprioception and Local Reflexes
In legged robotics (such as MIT Cheetah), reflexive control combining high backdrivability (joints rotating freely under external force) with proprioception has shown great success without force sensors. Manipulation has explored anti-slip reflexes using fingertip sensors, but this work achieves general geometric adaptation using only intrinsic kinematic history, avoiding expensive tactile sensors.

sections.heading: Training reflexes in simulation on three simple primitives
sections.summary: Three primitive environments—spring, plane, and rail—apply virtual forces to the end-effector during reinforcement learning with penalties on excess contact forces. Without force sensors, the policy outputs safe joint position offsets at 50 Hz using a 0.5-second history of joint motion.
sections.details:
### III-A Interaction Primitive Design
Contact tasks can be decomposed into constrained and unconstrained directions. To capture these, three virtual spring-damper models were created:
- **Spring**: An isotropic constraint pulling the end-effector back toward an arbitrary point in workspace.
- **Plane**: Produces normal reaction force based on penetration depth into a virtual wall, while leaving tangential translation completely unconstrained.
- **Rail**: A linear constraint in 3D space. It applies a restoring force perpendicular to the line based on deviation, while leaving motion along the line unconstrained.

### III-B Reflex Policy Reinforcement Learning
Training runs in simulation using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization). Given an end-effector target pose from above, the policy outputs joint position offsets $a_t$ at 50 Hz, passing $q_t^{\mathrm{ref}}$ to the low-level joint controller.

- **Observation Space**: Joint positions $q$, target joint errors $e^q$, commanded end-effector poses $p^d$, actual end-effector poses $p$ over the past 25 steps (0.5 s), and a compliance mode signal $m_t$. It observes no 6-axis F/T measurements or environmental geometry parameters.
- **Compliance Mode ($m_t$)**: A 1-bit switch indicating whether the robot should yield to contact (1) or track positions accurately in free space (0).
- **Key Reward Design**: It computes a "force-projected target position $x_t^c$," which pushes the commanded position $x_t^d$ back to where the static contact force remains below a threshold $F_{\mathrm{th}}$, rewarding tracking to $x_t^c$. Furthermore, a steep penalty (Excess-force cost) is applied whenever contact forces exceed the threshold, teaching the policy to offset joint targets in directions that release force.
- **Asymmetric Actor-Critic**: During training only, the critic receives ground-truth contact forces in simulation as privileged information, whereas the actor deployed on hardware receives only proprioceptive history.

sections.heading: Real-world and simulation validation: Lifting, ultra-precise insertion, and rough-surface following
sections.summary: Evaluated across humanoid dual-arm box lifting, 0.02 mm peg insertion with a QDD arm, and undulating surface following. Contact forces dropped significantly even with large command errors, maintaining high success rates where conventional IK and impedance control failed.
sections.details:
### IV-A Robot Setups and Low-Level Control
Experiments evaluated two platforms: a humanoid dual-arm system using high-ratio harmonic drives with model-based joint compliance control, and a custom 7-DoF Quasi-Direct Drive (QDD) arm with low gear ratios and inherent backdrivability.

### IV-B Dual-Arm Box Lifting
A task squeezing and lifting a box by its sides. Commanded penetration depth $d_{\mathrm{pen}}$ into the box surface was varied from 7.5 cm to 17.5 cm.
- With conventional inverse kinematics (IK + PD), joint tracking errors (indicating squeeze torque) escalated with penetration depth. At 17.5 cm, control diverged with severe oscillations, failing completely.
- In contrast, the reflex policy kept tracking errors below 12 degrees everywhere and safely completed lifts at all depths. It naturally learned to hold target joint positions near the box surface.

### IV-C Contact-Guided High-Precision Peg Insertion
A challenging task inserting a 12 mm diameter peg into holes with tiny clearances (0.1 mm and 0.02 mm), evaluated under initial hole position errors of 0 to 13 mm.
- Hardware experiments (Table II, Fig. 3): At 0.02 mm clearance and 9 mm position error, IK + PD achieved a 0% success rate (and at most 22% overall), whereas the reflex policy achieved 36–58% success. Moreover, mean estimated contact force was 6.3–7.6 N, less than half of IK + PD (17.4–20.0 N).
- Simulation evaluation (Table III): On unseen 0.02 mm clearance, the reflex policy achieved a 74.8% success rate, outperforming IK + PD (54.6%) and stiff impedance control. Ablation models trained without any single primitive (spring, plane, or rail) dropped to 46–68% success, proving the necessity of all three primitives.

### IV-D Unknown Rough-Surface Following
The robot traced an unknown undulating surface generated with Perlin noise ($\pm 20$ mm variation) under forced penetration commands of 15 to 45 mm (Fig. 4).
- Standard impedance control suffers: low stiffness degrades free-space tracking, while high stiffness spikes contact forces.
- The proposed method maintained low contact forces (95th percentile around 7.4 N, below the 10 N threshold) comparable to hybrid force-position control tuned for 5 N normal force, while smoothly following the surface. Crucially, it achieved this trade-off without being explicitly told which axis to force-control.

captions.F3: Peg insertion on the real QDD arm. Descending from an offset initial position (1), exploring the surface in a spiral pattern (2), detecting edge catch (3), and gently wiggling to seat the peg without excessive force (4–5). Bottom right shows a failure case where the baseline jams at the edge.
captions.F4: Results on unknown rough-surface following. (A) Undulating surface with up to $\pm 20$ mm relief. (B, C) Contact forces (p95) stay below the 10 N threshold on both flat and rough surfaces even at 45 mm penetration. (D) Free-space tracking error vs. contact force trade-off. While classic baselines follow gain-tuning curves (dashed lines), our method (Ours) hits a favorable balance comparable to hybrid control with an explicitly designated force-control axis.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: A purely proprioceptive reflex policy drastically reduces excess contact forces and boosts task success in contact-rich manipulation. Extending this to rotational constraints and fully automating compliance mode switching remain key next steps.
sections.details:
This paper showed that a proprioceptive reflex policy, trained purely on simple interaction primitives in simulation, functions as an exceptionally effective execution layer for contact-rich manipulation. Without force sensors or prior geometric models, it compliantly absorbs deep penetrations and jams during peg searches directly at the joint level.

However, three main limitations remain for future work:
- **Task Scope**: Verifying generalization across a broader and more diverse set of manipulation tasks.
- **Rotational Constraints**: Current primitives address only translational forces and constraints, not handling coupled translation-rotation constraints like door opening.
- **Mode Signal Dependence**: The compliance mode ($m_t$), which switches between free-space tracking and contact compliance, currently requires an external signal. Future work could enable the robot to adaptively switch modes online directly from proprioceptive history.

takeaways: You do not need to simulate complex full-task environments; training on minimal constraint models—spring, plane, and rail—is sufficient to acquire practical contact-adaptive reflexes.
Without 6-axis force/torque sensors, joint offsets that relieve excessive loads can be accurately inferred at 50 Hz purely from a 0.5-second history of joint angles and tracking errors.
Freezing this learned "reflex layer" between high-level task generation (planners or RL policies) and low-level joint control provides an exceptionally robust safety net against positional errors.
limitations: The constraint primitives are limited to translation, so the policy cannot directly handle contact tasks involving rotational constraints, such as tool orientation alignment or door hinges.
A 1-bit "compliance mode" signal indicating whether to comply or track strictly must be provided externally by high-level logic or heuristic thresholds.
The robot arm itself must possess some degree of passive compliance (e.g., backdrivability or accurate model-based joint torque control).
